option: Unity 6.x (LTS line, Unity 7 due Q1 2027) vs Unreal Engine 5.8 — head-to-head audit for Gacha Survivors. Recommendation: UNITY.
oneLine: Unity is the correct choice of the two and clears every hard requirement in the spec (it is literally the engine Vampire Survivors, Megabonk, 20 Minutes Till Dawn and DRG: Survivor all ship on), but it costs a full JS→C# port plus a handful of GUI-editor steps an AI agent cannot perform from text; Unreal is a poor fit bordering on disqualified — it has no web export at all since UE 4.24, its 2D stack (Paper2D) has been unmaintained-in-practice for the better part of a decade, and every one of its assets is a binary .uasset an agent cannot read or write.
strengths: [UNITY] Genre-proven at exactly this scale: Vampire Survivors itself moved from Phaser to Unity at v1.6, and its Unity build reportedly uses plain GameObjects/MonoBehaviours + aggressive object pooling — no DOTS. Megabonk (solo dev, Unity) sold 1M copies in 2 weeks with 117k peak CCU. 20 Minutes Till Dawn (Unity, solo dev 'flanne') and Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor (Unity, Funday Games) are both Unity. This exact game shape has been shipped in Unity by solo devs repeatedly.

[UNITY] Licensing is now benign and stable: Runtime Fee cancelled outright (Sept 2024), Personal free to $200k revenue+funding, no royalty ever, splash screen removable on Personal in Unity 6. The 2026 change was a 5% Pro price bump — not a structural change.

[UNITY] Assets are text. Scenes (.unity), prefabs (.prefab), ScriptableObjects (.asset), ProjectSettings, and Packages/manifest.json are YAML/JSON on disk. An AI agent can read them, diff them, and in many cases write them. This is the single biggest workflow difference from Unreal.

[UNITY] The game can be built ~90-95% code-first: one scene, one bootstrap MonoBehaviour, everything else spawned from C#. Sprites via Sprite.Create on a runtime Texture2D, materials via new Material(Shader.Find(...)), procedural SFX via AudioClip.Create (a direct analog of the spec's WebAudio synthesis), UI via UI Toolkit whose UXML/USS are text files. Prefab/inspector wiring is optional, not mandatory.

[UNITY] Headless harness maps cleanly: `-batchmode -nographics` builds plus System.Environment.GetCommandLineArgs() reproduce `?sim=1&char=rin&stage=2&seed=42` as CLI flags, and the spec's already-decoupled fixed-timestep sim means 100x speed is just 'call Step() 100 times per frame with no renderer'.
[UNITY] Best publishing surface of any engine: Steam, Switch/Switch 2, PS5, Xbox, iOS, Android, and a real (if heavy) web target. Unity 6 added mobile browser support to the Web platform.
[UNITY] Official Unity MCP server (in the com.unity.ai.assistant package) plus mature community MCP bridges let an agent drive the editor for the residual GUI work.

[UNREAL] Royalty terms are genuinely generous for a small game: 5% only after $1M lifetime gross per product, nothing owed in any quarter under $10k, and Epic Games Store sales are royalty-free and don't count toward the $1M. A game earning under $1M pays Epic literally nothing.
[UNREAL] Console pipeline is first-class and free of Unity's Pro-license gate — no seat cost to publish on console (platform-holder approval still required).

[UNREAL] UE 5.8 shipped an experimental first-party Unreal MCP plugin that embeds an MCP server in the editor process, exposing Blueprints, actors, materials and automation tests to Claude Code/Cursor. It is real, but experimental and requires a live editor.
dealbreakers: [UNREAL — hard disqualifier vs the spec] No web export exists. Epic removed HTML5 in UE 4.24; UE5 has never had a WASM/WebGL target. Pixel Streaming is server-rendered video, not a build, and costs GPU-hours per concurrent player. The spec's 'opens from index.html, no build step' requirement and any itch.io/browser demo — a primary discovery channel for survivors-likes — are permanently gone.

[UNREAL] Paper2D is maintained only in the sense that it still compiles. The Epic forum threads asking whether development stopped date to 2016-2017 and never received an Epic answer; the ecosystem's actual 2D animation solution is PaperZD, a third-party Fab plugin by an individual (Critical Failure Studio), which is what everyone building 2D in UE actually depends on. Your 2D animation stack would be a paid third-party plugin maintained by one person.

[UNREAL] Every asset is a binary .uasset — sprites, flipbooks, materials, DataTables, Blueprints, levels. An AI coding agent writing text files cannot create, read, diff, or merge any of them. Blueprint logic compiles to Kismet VM bytecode and cannot be recovered from disk. Every asset operation must proxy through a running editor over MCP; there is no offline path. Even Epic's own Developer Assistant reportedly covers only C++ and Verse, not Blueprints.

[UNREAL] C++ iteration speed is the wrong shape for an AI agent loop. Agents work by making many small edits and immediately re-verifying; UE full C++ rebuilds on a mid-range laptop run into minutes, header changes force wide rebuilds, and Live Coding is fast but unreliable for structural changes. Unity's domain reload for a project this size is seconds.

[UNREAL] A blank packaged UE5 project is ~300MB+; real projects routinely land at 5-15GB. For a game whose entire art budget is emoji and procedural shapes, that is an absurd download and a bad look on Steam and mobile.

[UNREAL] 2,000 AActors with PaperSpriteComponents is the wrong architecture — each sprite component is its own primitive with its own render proxy, so they don't batch. Getting to 2,000 requires abandoning Paper2D for a hand-rolled UPrimitiveComponent, Niagara, or Mass Entity (still experimental/WIP). You'd be writing your own 2D renderer inside a 3D engine — i.e. the exact work the Canvas2D spec already does, with none of the payoff.

[UNITY] The spec's zero-build-step, zero-dependency, opens-from-a-file property dies. Unity Web builds are ~8MB minimum, load slower than a hand-written Canvas game, and require a build step. If 'ships instantly on itch.io and loads in 2 seconds' is load-bearing for this project, Unity is a downgrade from the current plan.

[UNITY] Xbox publishing effectively requires Unity Pro ($2,310/seat/yr after the Jan 12 2026 increase). Sony and Nintendo issue Preferred Platform license keys that cover the console modules; Microsoft does not. Steam/mobile/web need nothing.

[UNITY] Emoji rendering is the one genuinely annoying gap. There is no Canvas 'fillText("🦈")' equivalent — you either generate a TextMeshPro font asset (a GUI wizard an agent cannot run headlessly), rasterize emoji to a texture at runtime, or bake an emoji atlas offline. Budget real time for this; it touches every entity's default look.

[BOTH] Neither engine is the best available answer. Two of the four biggest survivors-likes — Brotato (Blobfish) and Halls of Torment (Chasing Carrots) — shipped on Godot, whose .tscn/.tres scene and resource files are plain text and therefore the most AI-agent-friendly engine of the three. If the question were 'which engine' rather than 'Unity or Unreal', Godot deserves a seat at the table, and 'stay on HTML5/Canvas and ship' deserves one too.

facts.claim: Unity cancelled the Runtime Fee entirely in September 2024. Unity Personal remains free and its revenue+funding ceiling was doubled from $100,000 to $200,000. The 'Made with Unity' splash screen became optional for Personal users on Unity 6.
facts.source: https://unity.com/blog/unity-is-canceling-the-runtime-fee (via search result summary; corroborated by https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/unity-is-killing-its-controversial-runtime-fee and https://www.cgchannel.com/2024/09/unity-scraps-controversial-runtime-fee-but-raises-prices/)

facts.claim: Effective January 12, 2026, Unity Pro rose 5% from $2,200 to $2,310 per seat/year ($200→$210/month); Enterprise also rose 5%. This is the first price rise since the Runtime Fee was scrapped, and Unity's CEO committed to annual-only adjustments.
Unity thresholds as of 2026: Personal $0-$200k annual revenue+funding; Pro required above $200k; Enterprise required above $25M. There is no royalty or revenue share at any tier.
facts.source: https://unity.com/products/pricing-updates (via search summary; page 403s to direct fetch) and https://80.lv/articles/unity-announces-its-upcoming-2026-price-changes

facts.claim: Other 2026 Unity changes: Unity Version Control free cloud seats go from 3 to unlimited and free cloud storage from 5GB to 25GB by end of Q1 2026; Havok Physics is removed from Pro/Enterprise/Industry bundles starting Unity 6.3.

Unity 7 was announced at Unite Seoul 2026: early beta December 2026, full release Q1 2027, built incrementally on the Unity 6.x line (6.5 current, then 6.6 and 6.7 LTS), with an explicit promise of no project rebuilds, no new scripting language, and no broken workflows on upgrade.
facts.source: https://unity.com/news/unity-7-roadmap-revealed-at-unite-seoul and https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260720250213/en/Unity-7-Roadmap-Revealed-At-Unite-Seoul (unity.com pages 403 to direct fetch; sourced from search summaries + Inven Global and gamedeveloper.com coverage)

facts.claim: Unreal Engine is free for game development with a 5% royalty on worldwide gross revenue above the first $1,000,000 in LIFETIME gross revenue per product (the threshold does not reset annually). No royalty is owed in any calendar quarter where the product earns under $10,000.
facts.source: https://www.unrealengine.com/eula/unreal and https://www.unrealengine.com/license (via search summaries; both 403 to direct fetch) — corroborated by https://blog.promise.legal/game-engine-licensing-unity-runtime-fee/

facts.claim: Epic Games Store sales are royalty-free and do not count toward the $1M threshold. The 'Launch Everywhere with Epic' program reduces the royalty rate from 5% to 3.5% if you ship on EGS at or before other stores on the same platform.

Epic removed HTML5 export from Unreal in UE 4.24 due to low adoption. No HTML5/WebAssembly target has ever existed in UE5. Epic's recommended browser answer is Pixel Streaming (server-side rendering, video streamed to the client). Only unofficial community forks (e.g. SimplyStream's WASM+WebGPU work for UE 5.1-5.4) offer anything else.
Vampire Survivors used Phaser 3 + RexPlugins pre-v1.6, then Luca Galante announced in March 2022 a port to an 'industry-standard' engine; the game has run on Unity from v1.6 onward.

Vampire Survivors' Unity codebase uses plain GameObjects/MonoBehaviours with inheritance hierarchies, singleton GameManagers, Zenject DI, and a centralized object pool — NOT DOTS/ECS. Object pooling is credited as what enables its enemy counts.
facts.source: https://medium.com/@simon.nordon/unity-case-study-vampire-survivors-806eed11bebb (third-party decompile-based case study, not a developer statement)

facts.claim: Halls of Torment (Chasing Carrots) is built in GODOT, not Unity — it was the studio's first Godot title. Do not assume Unity here.
Brotato (Blobfish / Thomas Gervraud) is built in GODOT — the developer's first Godot game; it is featured in Godot's official showcase.
20 Minutes Till Dawn (flanne) is Unity. Shipped Windows, macOS, Android, iOS, and Nintendo Switch — a direct precedent for the Steam+mobile+console path from a solo dev.
Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor (Funday Games) is Unity. Early access Feb 14 2024, 1.0 on Sept 17 2025 for Windows and Xbox Series X/S.

Soulstone Survivors (Game Smithing) is Unity and does NOT use DOTS/ECS — it uses vanilla GameObject-Component architecture with an Entity.cs component holding pre-serialized references to every component it could have, to avoid runtime TryGetComponent cost. ~1400 scripts, hundreds of enemy prefabs.
facts.source: https://medium.com/@simon.nordon/unity-case-study-soulstone-survivors-f46ecf968845 (third-party analysis); community thread https://steamcommunity.com/app/2066020/discussions/0/4811561152898806514/ shows players demanding ECS and no official dev confirmation either way

facts.claim: Megabonk — solo developer 'Vedinad', Unity — released Sept 18 2025 and sold over one million copies in two weeks with a 117,336 peak CCU. The strongest single data point that one person + Unity + this genre works commercially.

DOTS/ECS is not required at 2,000 entities. Unity's Entities package targets counts an order of magnitude higher, and multiple developer reports find the Entities Graphics hybrid renderer SLOWER than GameObjects at modest counts. Separately, a non-DOTS Unity sprite renderer has been demonstrated at one million sprites above 120fps.

Unity stores scenes and prefabs as YAML text by default (Asset Serialization Mode: Force Text), which Unity explicitly recommends so version control can auto-merge them. Every asset carries a GUID in a sidecar .meta file that resolves all cross-references.

Unreal's .uasset binary format prevents AI agents from reading Blueprint logic, material graphs, UI layouts, or animation state machines from disk. Blueprints compile through a 9-stage pipeline to Kismet VM bytecode and are not recoverable from the file. Unreal's Python API lacks methods to create/connect individual Blueprint nodes, so every Unreal MCP server has independently reimplemented that missing API in a custom C++ plugin.
facts.source: https://www.sackbirdstudios.com/news/uasset-binary-problem (a studio blog with a clear pro-text-format thesis — treat the framing as advocacy, but the underlying technical claims about .uasset opacity and the missing Blueprint-node Python API match Epic's own docs and the state of the MCP ecosystem)

facts.claim: UE 5.8 ships an experimental first-party 'Unreal MCP' plugin that embeds an MCP server in the editor process over local HTTP, exposing actor spawning, lighting, material instances, Slate widget inspection, Blueprint work, and automation tests as tools for Claude Code / Cursor / Codex. Epic labels many features incomplete and the APIs subject to change.

Unity ships an official MCP server inside the com.unity.ai.assistant package connecting Claude Code, Cursor and others to the editor for project management, scene creation, asset management and code generation; Unity AI is in open beta for all Unity 6 developers. Mature community alternatives (ivanmurzak/unity-mcp, CoderGamester/mcp-unity) also exist.

Unity supports true headless execution via `-batchmode -nographics` (requires the Headless Build Support module for the editor). Note the constraint that `-executeMethod` can only invoke parameterless methods, so CLI parameters must be read via System.Environment.GetCommandLineArgs() — which is exactly how you'd reproduce the spec's `?sim=1&char=rin&stage=2&seed=42`.

Unity 6's Web platform defaults to WebGL2 with WebGPU still experimental, and added mobile browser support. Minimum Unity WebGL build size is around 8MB even for an empty project, with load times slower than web-native engines. Unity 6 also raised the desktop browser memory cap to 4096MB.
facts.source: https://unity.com/blog/engine-platform/web-runtime-updates-enhance-browser-experience ; https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/webgl-browsercompatibility.html ; https://discussions.unity.com/t/near-term-status-of-unity-6-and-desktop-4gb-web-support/946967 (the ~8MB figure comes from a comparison blog, not Unity, so treat it as an order-of-magnitude figure)

facts.claim: Publishing to Nintendo Switch, PlayStation, or Xbox from Unity requires an active Unity Pro subscription OR a Preferred Platform license key from the platform holder. Sony and Nintendo issue those keys; Microsoft does not, so Xbox in practice requires paid Pro. Platform-holder developer approval is required regardless.

An empty UE5 project packages to roughly 300-321MB, and typical six-month projects with marketplace assets and plugins reach 5-15GB. Engine content cooked by default accounts for ~100-180MB before you add a single asset of your own.

Unreal's Mass Entity framework (Epic's in-house ECS, built by the AI team for crowd simulation and shown in The Matrix Awakens) is still work-in-progress/experimental and documented as suitable 'for specific stuff only' — not a production-ready general answer for 2,000 gameplay entities.

PaperZD — the de-facto 2D animation solution for Unreal, described by its own listing as 'the definitive answer to Unreal Engine's lack of animation support for 2D projects' — is a third-party Fab plugin by Critical Failure Studio, updated to UE 5.6 in June 2025. Epic's own Paper2D still ships and is documented through UE 5.8, but the community threads asking whether Epic has stopped developing it date to 2016-2017 and never got an Epic answer.

The most prominent commercial Paper2D shipment is Octopath Traveler (Acquire, UE4), an HD-2D hybrid using Paper2D sprites over 3D environments — not a pure-2D high-entity-count game. There is no shipped Unreal survivors-like to point to.
facts.source: https://levelup.gitconnected.com/what-is-paper-2d-f362a10ad03a (secondary source; I could not verify the Paper2D usage claim against an Acquire or Square Enix primary source)

entityPerfNotes:
UNITY — yes, comfortably, and DOTS/ECS is NOT required. This is the single most-asked question about the engine and the shipped evidence answers it: Vampire Survivors' Unity build reportedly runs plain GameObjects/MonoBehaviours plus a centralized object pool; Soulstone Survivors is explicitly vanilla GameObject-Component (its Entity.cs pre-serializes every possible component reference precisely to avoid runtime TryGetComponent cost); Megabonk is a solo-dev Unity game that sold a million copies. None of them are DOTS. DOTS only starts paying for itself around 50k-100k+ entities, and several developer reports find the Entities Graphics hybrid renderer slower than GameObjects at modest counts.

The architecture that gets you there in Unity is the architecture the spec ALREADY mandates, which is the good news:
(1) Rendering is a non-issue at 2k. Put every placeholder sprite on one atlas, one material, one sorting layer — Unity's sprite batching / SRP Batcher collapses it to a handful of draw calls. If you want headroom, skip GameObjects for enemies entirely and issue Graphics.RenderMeshInstanced / CommandBuffer.DrawMeshInstanced from one manager; that path scales to five figures on integrated graphics.
(2) The real CPU killer is 2,000 MonoBehaviour Update() calls — each is a managed→native interop crossing and Unity's per-object call overhead dominates long before your gameplay math does. The fix is exactly the spec's design: enemies/projectiles/gems are plain C# structs in pooled arrays, and ONE EnemyManager.Update() iterates them. GameObjects, if used at all, are dumb transform+SpriteRenderer shells you write positions into.
(3) Do NOT use Unity 2D physics (Rigidbody2D/Collider2D) for 2,000 entities — it will not hold 60fps. Use the spec's own 64px spatial hash, written in pure C#. This ports line-for-line and is strictly faster than anything the engine offers here.
(4) The spec's "zero allocation in the hot loop" maps directly onto C#: struct arrays, pooling, no LINQ, no foreach over interfaces (boxing), no string concat for damage numbers. Verify with the Unity Profiler's GC Alloc row — same discipline, better tooling than a browser heap profile.
Net: 2,000 entities on a mid-range laptop has large margin. 10,000 is reachable with the same architecture.

UNREAL — reachable, but only by abandoning the engine's 2D path. 2,000 AActors each carrying a UPaperSpriteComponent is the wrong shape: every sprite component is its own primitive with its own render proxy and does not batch with its neighbours, so the render thread drowns well before the game thread does, and per-actor Tick overhead is far heavier than a MonoBehaviour Update. Blueprint tick at that count is hopeless — C++ is mandatory, not optional. The workable routes are all advanced: a single custom UPrimitiveComponent that builds one dynamic mesh per frame (i.e. you write your own 2D sprite renderer inside a 3D engine), Niagara particles for the swarm (fast, but they're not gameplay entities and wiring collisions/HP back to them is painful), or Mass Entity — Epic's ECS, still documented as work-in-progress "for specific stuff only." There is no tutorial path, no shipped survivors-like precedent, and no Stack Overflow answer for "2,000 Paper2D sprites at 60fps." You would be doing the same work the Canvas2D spec already does, in C++, with minutes-long rebuilds, and getting a 300MB+ binary for it.
publishingPaths:
STEAM — both are trivial and equivalent. Unity: Steamworks.NET or Facepunch.Steamworks, both free and open-source, pure C# and text-file-only integration (an AI agent can do the whole thing). Unreal: official Online Subsystem Steam. No cost difference; Unity has no royalty, and this game will almost certainly never cross Unreal's $1M lifetime threshold, so Unreal is also effectively free. Neither engine is a differentiator here.

CONSOLES — Unreal is nominally better, Unity is cheaper in practice. Both need platform-holder developer approval and a signed NDA before you can even download the console modules. Unity: Switch/Switch 2, PS5 and Xbox all supported; requires Unity Pro ($2,310/seat/yr) OR a Preferred Platform license key. Sony and Nintendo hand those keys out; Microsoft does not, so Xbox effectively costs you Pro. Unreal: no engine-side seat fee at all. But note 20 Minutes Till Dawn (Unity) and Halls of Torment (Godot) both shipped Switch — this genre gets to console on lightweight engines routinely, usually via a porting house (Seaven Studio did Brotato's Switch port). Console is a year-two problem either way; don't let it drive the engine choice.

MOBILE — Unity wins decisively. Unity's iOS/Android pipeline is the industry default and 20 Minutes Till Dawn shipped both (published by Erabit on mobile). This matters more than usual for THIS game: a gacha meta-layer with pity, banners and daily currency is a mobile-native monetization shape, and touch controls are already in the spec. Unreal supports mobile but is heavy for a 2D game — a 300MB+ floor before content, plus thermal/battery cost from a renderer you aren't using.

WEB — Unity is mediocre, Unreal is nonexistent. Unity 6's Web platform defaults to WebGL2 (WebGPU experimental) and added mobile browser support; expect roughly an 8MB floor and load times noticeably worse than a hand-written Canvas game, but it is genuinely shippable to itch.io (well within itch's 500MB-unpacked / 1000-file limits). Unreal has NO web target — Epic deleted HTML5 in 4.24 and UE5 never had one. Pixel Streaming is not a web build; it is you renting a GPU per concurrent viewer. For a survivors-like, a free browser demo on itch.io is one of the genre's proven discovery channels, and choosing Unreal permanently forecloses it.

BOTTOM LINE ON PUBLISHING: Unity reaches every surface the spec cares about. Unreal reaches all of them except the web, and is oversized for mobile. If the plan is Steam-first with an itch.io demo and a possible mobile port, Unity is the only one of the two that covers the whole board.
portCostFromSpec:
Neither engine lets you keep a single line of the written spec's implementation — it is HTML5 + Canvas 2D + ES modules + localStorage, and both engines are C#/C++ with their own asset and build pipelines. So the honest framing is: how much of the DESIGN and ARCHITECTURE survives the language port?

UNITY — ~100% of the JavaScript is rewritten as C#, but ~75-85% of the spec transliterates line-for-line, because the spec was written in an engine-agnostic, data-oriented style that happens to be exactly how you'd write this in Unity anyway.
Survives essentially unchanged (just retyped in C#): the fixed-60Hz accumulator loop with interpolated rendering (write your own in Update — do NOT use FixedUpdate, because the 100x harness needs to step the sim manually); object pooling with zero allocation; the 64px spatial hash; mulberry32/xorshift128 with two independent streams; the gacha soft/hard pity and 50/50 state machine; the wave director; the damage choke point; status effects; XP gem merging at 400; the off-screen culling and teleport rules; the 60-damage-number cap with 200ms aggregation; the 800-particle cap; the entire /src/data content registry (characters, enemies, stages, waves, upgrades, relics, gacha, evolutions become plain static C# classes or JSON — deliberately NOT ScriptableObject .asset files, which would drag the work back into the inspector); the 19x4 ability pillar registry; the displayName()/DEV_MODE helper; the one-to-one ref unit test.
Needs real rework (call it 15-25%):
  • Rendering. Canvas 2D immediate-mode fillCircle/drawStar calls become either generated textures on a runtime atlas or meshes. The spec's `visual: {shape, color, outline, size, emoji}` data object survives verbatim; only the drawing backend changes. The SpriteAtlas drop-in path actually gets EASIER — Unity's Sprite/atlas system is the native case.
  • Emoji. The one genuinely painful item. No fillText equivalent. Either bake an emoji atlas offline (a script an agent can write), rasterize from a system font at runtime, or generate a TextMeshPro font asset in the GUI. Plan for this explicitly; it is the default look of every entity in the game.
  • Persistence. localStorage → a JSON blob at Application.persistentDataPath (not PlayerPrefs — you want the single file with schemaVersion + migration fn, which maps cleanly). Same shape, ~20 lines.
  • Audio. WebAudio synthesized SFX → AudioClip.Create with a procedurally filled float[] buffer. Direct analog, roughly the same amount of code.
  • Headless harness. `?sim=1&char=rin&stage=2&seed=42` → `GachaSurvivors.exe -batchmode -nographics -sim -char rin -stage 2 -seed 42`, parsed via System.Environment.GetCommandLineArgs() (note: -executeMethod only takes parameterless methods, so read args yourself). The 100x speed requirement is already satisfied by the spec's decoupled sim — call Step() N times, skip the renderer. Output to stdout. This works well and is arguably BETTER than the browser version, because you can fan it out across cores.
  • Input. The four input paths (keyboard/mouse/gamepad/touch) are one Input System action asset away — and .inputactions files are JSON text, so an agent can author them.
  • "Opens from index.html with no build step" — this acceptance criterion is deleted, permanently. Accept that or don't move.
EDITOR-GUI COST (the AI-agent question, quantified): if you deliberately build code-first, roughly 5-15% of the work lands in the GUI, nearly all of it one-time setup — create project, set Player/Quality settings, add packages, generate the emoji font asset, configure build targets. Everything else can be C# text files plus a single scene containing one bootstrap GameObject. Note that ProjectSettings/*.asset and Packages/manifest.json are themselves YAML/JSON, so even much of that is agent-editable, and the official Unity MCP server closes the rest. The trap to avoid is the "normal" Unity workflow — prefabs per enemy, ScriptableObjects per character, values wired in the inspector — which would push GUI work to 40%+ and hand your AI agent a codebase it can only half-see. Write it down as a project rule: no prefabs except the one bootstrap object, no inspector-authored data, all content in code or JSON.

UNREAL — ~100% rewritten AND the architecture changes. On top of everything above, you'd re-plan the entity system (Paper2D actors don't reach 2,000, so you write a custom primitive component or adopt experimental Mass Entity), rewrite the renderer against a 3D pipeline you don't need, and abandon the web target entirely. The headless harness has a good analog — a C++ commandlet run with -nullrhi -unattended against a cooked build — but it's a heavier setup than a CLI flag. The data registry should stay as C++ structs or JSON rather than DataTables, since DataTables are binary .uasset and therefore invisible to your agent. Add minutes-long C++ rebuild cycles on every iteration, a 300MB+ empty-project floor, and a 2D animation stack that depends on a one-person third-party Fab plugin. Realistically 1.5-2x the Unity effort for a strictly worse outcome on every axis this spec cares about.
